dom.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source accepts the application-layer thesis and materially develops it through a multi-model strategy: Harvey would route legal tasks to different foundation models, deepen task-specific evaluation and enable firm-specific workflow customisation. Its claimed performance benefits remain prospective, however, and it provides no measured evidence that these capabilities create durable defensibility.
qs: Multi-model integration will also open up novel customization and optimization options for firm-specific use cases and workflows.
We’re pairing this shift with deeper evaluations to help match users with the right models for the right legal tasks.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: Harvey’s proprietary benchmark reports broad improvement but explicitly limits the inference: results concern models optimized within Harvey, and aggregate gains coexist with substantial task-specific differences. This supports the cluster’s distinction between average benchmark success and dependable performance across complete legal work, although the source does not itself test strict end-to-end completion.
qs: The below graph shows performance of various models when incorporated into and optimized for Harvey systems.
There is still a substantial gap in which model is best suited to a particular* legal task.

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: Harvey supports task-specific legal-AI evaluation, arguing that aggregate scores obscure material differences across tasks and that expert assessment captures nuances missed by single-score benchmarks. It also links evaluation to use-case-specific model selection, though it does not directly address partial-credit inflation or demonstrate reproducibility.
qs: ### Quantifying Quality  Enabling a broad range of models for an even broader range of legal workflows requires novel evaluations suited to capturing task-specific variances that are becoming essential to pushing the quality frontier.
We will also begin to publish results of our expert evaluation process, where top lawyers provide nuanced insights into model performance not captured by single-score benchmarks.

kp.k: Harvey expands beyond OpenAI to multiple foundation-model providers
kp.d: In its May 13, 2025 announcement, Harvey describes incorporating and optimizing Anthropic and Google models alongside existing OpenAI models. Integration is through AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex, with Harvey asserting unchanged security and privacy guarantees. Further providers are a future intention rather than a completed expansion.
qs: The first change we are making is to incorporate and optimize leading foundation models from Anthropic and Google for use across the Harvey platform.

Both models will be integrated through their respective cloud providers (AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex), with the same [security and privacy guarantees](/en-US/security) that have always existed on the Harvey platform.
Over time, we intend to identify other foundation model providers that provide unique advantages for Harvey systems and incorporate them as well.

kp.k: Improved baseline reasoning shifts platform optimization toward execution
kp.d: Harvey argues that better general foundation-model legal reasoning reduces the effort required to adopt new models, allowing optimization to concentrate on task execution, firm knowledge and collaboration. On its proprietary BigLaw Bench, Harvey reports that, in less than a year, seven models, including three non-OAI models, outperform its originally benchmarked system when incorporated into and optimized for Harvey systems. This is a vendor-reported benchmark finding, not an independent evaluation.
qs: Since then, general foundation models have improved at baseline legal reasoning.

This dramatically reduces the effort of adopting new models into the Harvey platform, as optimization can be focused on task execution, incorporating firm knowledge, and user collaboration rather than baseline reasoning.
The below graph shows performance of various models when incorporated into and optimized for Harvey systems.
In less than a year, seven models (including three non-OAI models) now outperform the originally benchmarked Harvey system on BigLaw Bench.

kp.k: Legal task differences prevent a single best model
kp.d: Harvey reports substantial task-specific differences despite convergence in overall model quality. Its example is Gemini 2.5 Pro performing strongly in legal drafting but struggling with trial preparation and oral argument because of difficulty reasoning about complex evidentiary rules, including hearsay. Harvey uses these differences to argue for matching models to particular legal tasks rather than selecting one universally superior model.
qs: For example, on BigLaw Bench subtasks, Gemini 2.5 Pro excels at legal drafting but struggles at trial preparation and oral argument due to difficulties in reasoning effectively about complex evidentiary rules like hearsay which models from other providers understand more clearly.

Taken together, these different perspectives on evaluation point towards the same outcome: there is no longer a single “best” model, but an array of premier models, each particularly suited to different legal tasks and preferences.

kp.k: Expert preferences reflect presentation as well as answer quality
kp.d: Harvey reports wide variation in expert assessments of individual outputs even as aggregate assessments converge. It says tone, style and structure increasingly drive preferences when models arrive at the same answer. These are qualitative claims about expert evaluation; the document supplies no sample size or numerical preference results.
qs: When asked to consider response quality and preference, experts show a wide variance on individual model outputs even as their evaluations of model quality tend to converge at scale.

In an increasing number of cases, expert preference is also being driven by subjective factors such as tone, style, and structure as models converge on the right answer but present that answer in materially different forms.

kp.k: Automatic routing combines with lawyer-controlled model selection
kp.d: Harvey describes default routing to models selected for the work, alongside a model selector for lawyers and teams wanting direct control. It predicts better responses, more collaborative agents, stronger workflows and firm-specific customization from multi-model integration; the announcement does not quantify realized client outcomes from these changes.
qs: Most simply, users will continue to use Harvey as they normally do while seamlessly being routed to the best models for their work.
Lawyers and teams interested in more actively exploring how different models can support their work will also have access to a model selector.
This will allow them to pick the particular model used by Harvey’s model systems to support their work, or choose “auto” to have Harvey select for them.
Multi-model integration will also open up novel customization and optimization options for firm-specific use cases and workflows.

kp.k: Multi-step workflows require higher quality at each step
kp.d: Harvey argues that complex agents and workflows reduce the margin for error at each constituent step. It illustrates the mechanism with a three-step process in which completing 80% of the work at each step means completing only about half overall. This is an illustrative argument for task-specific model selection, not a reported measurement of deployed workflow performance.
qs: These multi-step problems demand increasingly exacting model quality as they considerably shrink the margin of error for each model.
Even on a relatively straightforward three-step process, completing 80% of the work at each step means only completing about half of the overall work.

kp.k: Specialized models can divide research, drafting and orchestration
kp.d: Harvey proposes decomposing legal workflows so that different models handle research, drafting, planning, orchestration and execution according to their strengths. It argues that task-specific systems can meet higher quality requirements without requiring each model to excel at every activity, and predicts that a broader model base will improve existing systems and enable new ones.
qs: When building a research agent, you don’t need to worry about whether a model struggles at writing; you can use a separate model to draft once the research is compiled.

Instead, you can identify the optimal solution for a particular workflow or even a particular step—independently choosing the model best suited to plan, orchestrate, and execute each task across a complex system.
Broadening the number of base models that the Harvey team can integrate will increase the quality of existing systems and allow for entirely new ones.

kp.k: Public benchmarks and expert evaluations will guide model choice
kp.d: Harvey commits to maintaining a public BigLaw Bench leaderboard and beginning publication of expert evaluation results. It presents these as complementary ways to track legal reasoning, capture nuances beyond single-score benchmarks and guide clients toward models suited to their use cases and preferences. These are announced evaluation commitments, distinct from human verification of AI output before reliance.
qs: Clear evaluations allow us to give precise insights on which models are best suited for particular use cases and preferences, and how Harvey systems overall help solve our clients’ unique problems.
To that end, we will be maintaining a public leaderboard for BigLaw Bench, providing an up-to-date standard on how baseline model reasoning is evolving on legal tasks.
We will also begin to publish results of our expert evaluation process, where top lawyers provide nuanced insights into model performance not captured by single-score benchmarks.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims that improving foundation models and task-specific model selection enable better legal AI systems, and predicts that multi-model integration will improve legal workflows and enable new functionality.
pts.d: The Harvey Team says baseline legal reasoning has improved enough to reduce the effort required to adopt additional models, allowing optimization to focus on execution, firm knowledge and collaboration. It reports that seven models optimized within Harvey systems outperform its originally benchmarked system. However, it argues that aggregate convergence conceals task-specific differences: Gemini 2.5 Pro performs strongly in drafting but struggles with trial preparation and oral argument involving complex evidentiary rules. Expert preferences also differ with tone, style and structure. On this basis, the team argues that there is no single best model for all legal work. It predicts that adding Anthropic and Google models alongside OpenAI models, with automatic routing or user selection, will improve responses, agents and workflows and permit firm-specific customization. It also predicts that selecting different models for planning, research, drafting and other workflow steps will improve existing systems and enable new ones.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source supports its claims with Harvey's proprietary BigLaw Bench, descriptions of expert evaluations and an illustrative argument about multi-step workflow reliability.
pts.d: The benchmark evidence concerns models incorporated into and optimized for Harvey systems, rather than an explicitly independent comparison of unmodified models. The text reports seven models exceeding the original Harvey system and gives a task-level example involving Gemini 2.5 Pro, but the supplied document does not provide numerical scores or detailed testing methods. The team also describes experts showing substantial variation in preferences for individual outputs despite convergence in aggregate assessments, with presentation increasingly influencing preference. The three-step example illustrates compounding performance requirements; it is not presented as a measured legal-workflow result. Improvements from broader integration and new functionality are prospective claims supported by these evaluations and system-design reasoning, not by reported client-outcome measurements. Harvey commits to publishing a BigLaw Bench leaderboard and expert evaluation results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The May 13, 2025 announcement distinguishes improvements already observed over less than a year from prospective integration, workflow and evaluation developments without fixed completion dates.
pts.d: The team describes the seven-model benchmark improvement as occurring in less than a year after its initial benchmark results. The article announces the addition of Anthropic and Google models while also using future-tense language about their integration and user access. It gives no precise rollout dates for model selection, the public leaderboard or expert evaluation publication. Further providers may be incorporated over time if they offer unique advantages. Predicted benefits depend on integrating and optimizing models within Harvey and matching their strengths to particular legal tasks or workflow steps. The team qualifies aggregate model-quality convergence by emphasizing task-specific weaknesses and subjective preferences. More complex multi-step workflows require increasingly high per-step quality. Integration through AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex is stated to retain existing security and privacy guarantees.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects primarily concern Harvey's lawyer users, legal teams and client firms, alongside Harvey's own system-development work.
pts.d: Most users are expected to benefit through automatic model routing without changing how they use Harvey. Lawyers and teams seeking more control will be able to select models themselves. Firms are promised customization for their knowledge, use cases and workflows. Users performing drafting, research, trial preparation and oral argument may benefit differently because model strengths vary across these tasks. Harvey's development team expects to spend less effort on baseline reasoning and more on execution, firm knowledge and collaboration, while using different models for different workflow stages. Clients are also expected to gain guidance from more detailed evaluations about which models fit their needs and preferences. The document does not make concrete predictions about legal employment, staffing structures, billing, market shares or access to justice.
